explain: 3sg + the -ā question ending
ఆకలి 'hunger' with -తో 'with'. Telugu describes this state as accompaniment — literally 'with hunger' — where English uses an adjective.
ఆడు 'to play' with -టం, which makes a verbal noun — the equivalent of English '-ing' used as a noun. It can then take case endings and act as a subject or object, as in ఆడటం ఇష్టం 'likes playing'.
Used with చేయు as ఆదా చేయు 'to save (money)'. Telugu forms a great many verbs by pairing a noun like this with చేయు 'do' or అవు 'become'.
ఆమె 'she' with the dative -కు. As with names, this is the form used for the person experiencing something: ఆమెకు ఇష్టం is 'she likes it', literally 'to her it is a liking'.
ఆలోచిస్తున్నాడు 'he is thinking' (present continuous) plus the question marker.
ఆహారం in the accusative
The language name as borrowed and used in ordinary speech.
ఇల్లు in its oblique form
The oblique stem ఇంట్‌ of ఇల్లు 'house', plus the locative -లో, plus -నూ 'also'. Note ఇల్లు changes shape before endings — an irregularity worth memorising, since the word is very common.

gloss: at home itself / right at home
explain: ఇల్లు 'house' takes the oblique stem ఇంట్‌, adds the locative -లో, then the emphatic -ఏ. That final vowel means 'precisely, none other' — staying *at home* rather than going anywhere.
habitual/future, 3pl of ఇష్టపడు
ఇష్టం 'liking, fondness' with the yes/no question marker -ఆ. Adding this single vowel to the end of a statement turns it into a question, with no change in word order.
ఉంటాడు 'he is' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.
habitual/future, 3pl of ఉండు
ఉంటారు 'they are' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.
3sg + the -ā question ending
The whole 'wants to' chain — ఉండాలి 'must stay' + అని + అనుకుంటున్నాడు 'he is thinking' — with the question marker on the end. Only the last element takes it, however long the chain.
The same 'wants to' chain turned into a noun with -డం, so it can be negated as a whole: ఉండాలనుకోవడం లేదు, 'there is no wanting to stay'.

The conjunctive participle of ఉండు 'to be, to stay'. Telugu chains actions with this form instead of repeating a finite verb: ఇంట్లోనే ఉండి ... చేయాలని is 'staying at home and ...'. Only the last verb in such a chain carries person and tense.
The habitual relative participle of ఉండు. Where ఉన్న describes a state now, ఉండే describes what is generally or characteristically the case: స్నేహంగా ఉండే వాళ్ళు, 'people who are friendly'.
ఉంది '(it) is, there is' with the yes/no marker -ఆ. Telugu has no verb 'to have': possession is expressed as existence, so డస్టిన్‌కు ... ఉందా is literally 'to Dustin, does there exist ...?'
ఉత్సాహం 'enthusiasm, excitement' with the adverbial -గా, pairing with ఉండటం to describe a state: ఉత్సాహంగా ఉన్నాడు 'he is excited'.

The relative participle of ఉండు 'to be'. Telugu has no relative pronouns; instead the verb takes this form and sits directly before the noun it modifies: ఆకలితో ఉన్న కస్టమర్లు, 'customers who are hungry'.
ఉన్నాడు 'he is' plus the question marker. ఉన్నాడు describes a state right now, where ఉంటాడు describes what is generally so.
3pl + the -ā question ending
ఎక్కడికి + ఐనా
ఏడు "seven" + అన్నర "and a half"
ఏడు 'seven' plus అన్నర 'and a half', with the dative -కు for clock time. Telugu builds half-hours with this -అన్నర rather than a separate word for 'thirty'.
The name ఏమీ with the dative -కి. -కి rather than -కు because the name ends in a front vowel — the two are the same ending, chosen by the preceding sound.
Literally 'one to one' — ఒకరు 'one person' in the dative, then ఒకరు again. Telugu builds the reciprocal by repeating the word rather than with a separate pronoun like English 'each other'.
కంప్యూటర్ with the locative -లో. Telugu uses 'in' where English says 'on' for this.

కథ 'story' with the accusative ending -ను, which marks it as the thing being acted on. Telugu adds -ను/-ని to definite or animate objects; an indefinite object often takes no ending at all. Dictionary form: కథ.
కనిపిస్తుంది 'it appears, is visible' plus the question marker. Telugu often frames seeing this way — the thing seen is the subject and the seer takes the dative.
A borrowing from English 'cup', long naturalised.
కలువు 'to meet' with -గల-, which marks ability, plus the third-person masculine ending. This -గల- is Telugu's 'can': it slots between the stem and the person ending, so కలవగలను is 'I can meet'.
కలువు with the ability marker -గల- and the first-person ending -ను.
కస్టమర్ with the oblique plural -ల, the form used before another ending or postposition — here before కోసం 'for'.
కస్టమర్ plus the plural -ల plus -తో 'with'. Telugu stacks these in a fixed order: stem, number, then case.
కస్టమర్ 'customer' with the plural ending -లు. The borrowed singular takes native Telugu plural and case endings exactly as a Telugu noun would.

pos: the negative copula కాదు + the -ā question ending

explain: కారు 'car' with the locative -లో. Telugu uses this for the means of travel where English says 'by car'.
The English name Karen in Telugu script, inflecting like any noun: కారెన్‌కు 'to Karen'.

కారెన్ plus the dative ending -కు. Telugu uses the dative far more widely than English 'to' — it also marks the experiencer of a feeling, so కారెన్‌కు విసుగ్గా ఉంటుంది is literally 'to Karen it is boring', i.e. Karen is bored.
present continuous + the -ā question ending
present continuous, 3sg fem — కావాలి + అనుకో
కావాలి 'is wanted, is needed' plus the question marker. What is wanted is the grammatical subject and the wanter takes the dative, so కారెన్‌కు ... కావాలా is 'to Karen, is ... wanted?'
కాసేపు + the dative -కి
"ఖర్చుతో కూడుకున్నది" = involves expense
కూతురు + అంటే, the subject of a liking
కూతురు + the dative -కి
కూతురు 'daughter' with the dative -కు, here in the possession pattern: కూతురుకు ... ఉన్నారు, 'the daughter has ...'.
కొను 'to buy' with the first-person ending -తాను.
కొంటుంది 'she buys' plus the question marker.
కొను 'to buy' with -తుంది, the third-person ending for a feminine or neuter subject in the habitual/future. The masculine counterpart would be కొంటాడు.
Used before a noun for an unspecified quantity. The related కొంతమంది means 'some people'.
present continuous + the -ā question ending
present continuous; with బోర్ = "is bored"
కొద్ది "little" + సేపు "time"

obligative of కొను

past, 1sg of కొను
The English name Clare in Telugu script. Like other borrowed names it takes ordinary case endings — క్లేర్‌కు 'to Clare'.
క్లేర్ with the dative -కు, for the recipient or the experiencer of a state.
Names the cost of something, and by extension is used predicatively for 'expensive': చాలా ఖరీదు, 'costs a lot'.

ఖరీదు 'price, cost' plus -ఐన, which makes an adjective, plus -ది, which turns that adjective back into a standalone noun-like predicate. Telugu often ends an equational sentence with this -ది where English would just use 'is'.
ఖరీదు "price" + -ఐన
గంట 'hour' with the plural -ల and the dative -కు. Telugu tells clock time with the dative: ఆరు గంటలకు is 'at six o'clock'. The dative here marks a point in time rather than a recipient.
The native Telugu word for mathematics. Everyday school speech often uses the borrowed మ్యాథ్స్ instead; both are current.
చదువు 'to read' with -డం, which makes a verbal noun. Like ఆడటం 'playing', it can head a phrase and take case endings — చదవడం ఇష్టం, 'likes reading'.

చదువు 'to read, to study' with the reflexive -కొని and the conjunctive ending — 'having studied (for oneself)'. The conjunctive participle chains actions; only the final verb in the chain carries tense and person.
చదువుకొను 'to study (for oneself)' in its obligative form with the quotative అని, giving the content of the decision.
చదువు 'to study' with -తాము, first person plural.
habitual/future, 3sg fem + the -ā question ending
చూడు 'to see, watch' with the verbal-noun -టం, the same ending as ఆడటం 'playing'.

marks who is made to do something
చేయ-, the bare stem of చేయు, with అవసరం 'necessity'. It usually appears negated — చేయనవసరం లేదు, 'there is no need to do', i.e. doesn't have to.

gloss: intending to do / that (one) should do
explain: చేయాలి 'must do' with the quotative అని. This pairing introduces an intention or a purpose, and is what the preceding clause is 'about' when it ends in నిర్ణయించుకుంటాడు 'decides'.
చేయిస్తుంది, the causative, plus the question marker.

చేయు 'to do' in its causative form: -ఇంచు/-ఇస్తు inserts a second participant who causes the action. The person made to act takes -తో: జాన్‌తో హోంవర్క్ చేయిస్తుంది, 'she makes Jon do the homework'. This causative is fully productive across Telugu verbs.
past, 1sg of చేయు
past, 3sg fem + the -ā question ending
The first-person plural of చేసుకుంటారు.
చేయు with the reflexive -కొను and the third-person plural ending. The reflexive is what makes ఒకరికొకరు సహాయం చేసుకుంటారు mean they help *each other* rather than someone else.

చేయు 'to do, make' with the reflexive -కొను and the conjunctive ending. The reflexive marks the action as done for one's own benefit, which is why it fits 'makes his breakfast' better than plain చేసి would.
habitual/future, 3sg masc + the -ā question ending
చేస్తుంది 'she does' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.
చౌకైనది 'is a cheap one' plus the question marker.
చౌక 'cheap' with -ఐన making an adjective and -ది making it a standalone predicate — the same construction as ఖరీదైనది, its opposite.
The English name Jon in Telugu script, inflecting like any noun: జాన్‌కు 'to Jon'.
జాన్ with the dative -కు. Used for the recipient, and for the one experiencing a state: జాన్‌కు హోంవర్క్ ఉంది, 'Jon has homework', literally 'to Jon there is homework'.
జాన్ with -తో 'with'. In a causative sentence this same -తో marks the person who is made to do something, not a companion.
The name జూలీ plus the question marker, with -న- inserted between the two vowels so they do not collide — a regular Telugu adjustment.
The borrowed టికెట్ with the native plural -లు.
టీచర్ 'teacher' with the plural -ల and the dative -కు. Used in the experiencer pattern: టీచర్లకు ... ఇష్టం, 'the teachers like ...'.
The English name Dustin in Telugu script, inflecting normally: డస్టిన్‌కు 'to Dustin'.
డస్టిన్ with the dative -కు, used both for 'to Dustin' and for Dustin as the one experiencing something — డస్టిన్‌కు ఫ్రెంచ్ రాదు, 'French doesn't come to Dustin', i.e. he doesn't speak French.
తాగుతాడు 'he drinks' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.
habitual/future, 3pl + the -ā question ending
past, 1pl of తిను
habitual/future, 3sg masc + the -ā question ending
తెలియు 'to be known' with the negative -దు. Knowledge is expressed impersonally: the thing known is the subject and the knower takes the dative, so అతనికి తెలియదు is 'to him it is not known'.
past, 3sg masc + the -ā question ending
past, 3sg masc of తోముకో
దుకాణం + the dative -కి
దుకాణం in the accusative

దేశం 'country' with the plural -ల in its oblique form — the shape a plural takes before another ending or postposition. Here it precedes నుంచి 'from': చాలా దేశాల నుంచి, 'from many countries'. Note the plural is -ల, not the -లు that ends a standalone plural.
past + the -ā question ending
నడుచు 'to walk' with the reflexive -కొను and the durative -తూ, describing an action ongoing while something else happens. -తూ is Telugu's 'while X-ing'.
నేను 'I' takes the oblique నా before -తో 'with'.
past, 3pl, causative of నిద్రపో
habitual/future, 1pl, causative
past, 3sg masc of నిద్రపో
నిర్ణయించుకుంటాడు 'he decides' plus the question marker.
నిర్ణయించు 'to decide' with the reflexive -కొను, marking that the decision is for and about himself. Telugu uses this reflexive far more than English does.
నిర్ణయించుకొను 'to decide (for oneself)' with the first-person ending.
past, 3sg masc + the -ā question ending
past, 3sg masc of నిర్ణయించుకో
past, 1sg of నిర్ణయించుకో

నీళ్లు 'water' (grammatically plural in Telugu) plus అంటే, literally 'if (one) says'. It marks the topic of a feeling: నీళ్లంటే భయం is 'as for water, (there is) fear' — the standard way to say someone is afraid of something.
నేను 'I' plus అంటే 'if (one) says', marking the topic. నేనంటే ఇష్టం is 'as for me, (there is) liking' — the standard frame for saying someone likes a person.
నేర్చుకో + -ఆలని "in order to / that one should"

pos: "ఇంటి పట్టునే" = at home and nowhere else

explain: habitual/future, 3sg masc + the -ā question ending
పని 'work, task' with the dative -కి, marking destination. Note -కి rather than -కు: the choice follows the preceding vowel, with -కి after front vowels like the ి of పని.
పని 'work' with the locative -లో.
పని 'work' plus the locative -లో plus -నూ 'also'. The -నూ ending pairs across a list: పనిలోనూ ఇంట్లోనూ is 'both at work and at home'.
పని 'work, task' with the plural -లు. The singular means work in general; the plural counts individual tasks.
"రెండు వారాల పాటు" = for two weeks
పిల్లి 'cat' with the accusative -ని. Animate objects reliably take this ending in Telugu, where an inanimate one might not. Dictionary form: పిల్లి.
"పెంపుడు జంతువుల దుకాణం" = pet store
The English word 'pet', used here in the compound పెట్ షాప్ 'pet shop'. Borrowed compounds like this are usual in urban speech.
habitual/future, 3sg masc of పెట్టు
పొద్దున 'morning' with the emphatic -ఏ, giving 'in the morning itself', i.e. early. That final -ఏ meaning 'precisely, none other' is the same one in ఇంట్లోనే.
past, 1sg of పో
past, 3sg fem-neut of పో
ప్రజలు in the accusative
ప్రతి "every" + రోజు "day" + emphatic -ū
past, 1sg of ప్రయత్నించు
past, 3sg fem of ప్రయత్నించు
ప్రయత్నించు 'to try' with -తాను, first person singular.
ప్రయత్నించు 'to try' with -తుంది, third person feminine/neuter. What is tried takes the dative: ...చేయడానికి ప్రయత్నిస్తుంది, 'tries to do ...'.
The country name in Telugu script, inflecting like any noun: ఫ్రాన్స్‌కు 'to France'.
ఫ్రాన్స్ with the dative -కు marking destination.
The language name borrowed from English. Telugu names languages with this borrowed form in ordinary speech, and pairs them with రావడం 'to come' rather than 'to speak' when talking about ability.
బంధువులు 'relatives' plus the question marker.
బంధువు 'relative' with the plural -లు. Covers kin generally, without specifying the relationship.
the native Telugu word; the stories also use షూలు
The English word, used here in బెస్ట్ ఫ్రెండ్. This borrowing is at least as common in casual speech as the more literary ప్రాణ స్నేహితురాలు.
English "boring" + -గా
"బోర్ కొడుతోంది" = it is boring
English "break" with the Telugu plural -లు
భాష 'language' with the plural -లు.
మంది, the counter used for people, with the accusative -ని. Telugu counts humans with మంది rather than a bare number: చాలా మందిని, 'many people' as an object.
మాట్లాడు 'to speak' with -తారు, third person plural habitual.

మాట్లాడు 'to speak' with the past participle -ిన and అప్పుడు 'at the time'. Telugu builds 'when X' clauses this way rather than with a conjunction — the -ిన form is not really past here, it simply marks the event the timing hangs on.
"at the time of speaking", from మాట్లాడు

The English name Mike written in Telugu script, so the sound is preserved rather than the spelling. Names are transliterated in this project rather than left in Latin letters, which means they inflect like any Telugu noun: మైక్‌కి 'to Mike'.
Marks the first item in a sequence of events. Pairs with తర్వాత 'afterwards, then'.
మొదలవుతుంది 'it starts' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.

మొదలు 'beginning' with అవుతుంది '(it) becomes' — Telugu forms many verbs by pairing a noun with అవు 'become' or చేయి 'do'. The -ుంది ending is third person singular for a non-masculine subject, which is why 'work' takes it here.
The negative of మొదలవుతుంది. Telugu negates by replacing the tense ending rather than adding a separate word — there is no equivalent of 'does not' standing on its own.
Borrowed from English and used as an ordinary noun.
the translator writes it this way; a learner may read it as ఏమి "what"
రాణించు 'to excel' with the first-person plural ending.
రాణించు 'to shine, to excel' with -తారు, third person plural. Also the polite form for a single person.
రాణిస్తుంది 'she does well' plus the question marker.
రుచి 'taste' with the adverbial -గా, pairing with ఉండటం: రుచిగా ఉండదు, 'it is not tasty'.
The borrowed రెస్టారెంట్ with the locative -లో 'in, at'. Consonant-final loanwords take native case endings unchanged.
లేస్తాడు 'he gets up' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.
లేచు 'to rise, get up' with -స్తాడు, third person masculine in the habitual/future. Telugu uses one tense for both habit and future; context distinguishes them.
లేచు 'to rise' with -తాను, first person singular. The third-person counterpart is లేస్తాడు.
వంటమనిషి plus the question marker.
వంట 'cooking' plus మనిషి 'person'. Unlike వంటవాడు, which is specifically masculine, మనిషి is gender-neutral in form and so serves for a woman.
వంటవాడు plus the question marker. Because Telugu needs no copula, questioning an equational sentence means attaching -ఆ straight to the predicate noun.

వంటవాడు 'cook' in the form used when the speaker is the one being described. Telugu marks the predicate noun for person in an equational sentence: వంటవాడు 'he is a cook' becomes వంటవాడిని 'I am a cook'.

వంట 'cooking' plus -వాడు, the masculine agent suffix — literally 'cooking-man'. The feminine counterpart is వంటమనిషి or వంటది depending on region. -వాడు is a productive way to name someone by what they do.

gloss: does (he) know it? / did it come?
explain: వచ్చు 'to come' with the question marker. In the language-ability idiom, ఫ్రెంచ్ వచ్చా is 'does French come (to him)?', i.e. does he speak French — the same రావడం idiom as రాదు.
వస్తారు 'they come' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.

pos: the -వాడు agent ending + the -ā question ending

explain: వారాలు in its oblique form
వారం 'week' with the plural -లు.
విద్యార్థి 'student' plus the question marker.
విద్యార్థిని 'female student' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.

The feminine counterpart of విద్యార్థి 'student'. Telugu marks gender on many agent nouns this way, and the verb agrees with it. Note the trap: this looks identical to a noun carrying the accusative -ని, but here the ending is part of the word itself.

విధం 'manner, way' plus -గా, the suffix that turns a noun or adjective into an adverb. వేరే విధంగా is 'in a different way'. This -గా is one of the most productive endings in the language — the same move gives సంతోషంగా 'happily' and స్నేహంగా 'in a friendly way'.

విసుగు 'boredom' with the adverbial -గా. It appears with ఉండటం in the dative-experiencer pattern: someone-కు విసుగ్గా ఉంటుంది, 'to them it is boring'. Telugu expresses this state as something happening to a person, not something they do.

వెళ్తాడు 'he goes' plus the question marker. The final -ఆ is Telugu's yes/no question marker: attach it to the end of a statement and the word order does not change at all.
వెళ్తుంది 'she goes' plus the question marker.
వెళ్ళు 'to go' with the durative -తూ. Chains with another verb to say two things happened at once: నడుచుకుంటూ వెళ్తూ ... చూస్తుంది, 'walking along, she sees ...'.
వెళ్ళాలి 'must go' with the quotative అని, introducing the content of a thought or intention — what he is thinking *about*.

Three pieces fused: వెళ్ళాలి 'must/should go', the quotative అని, and అనుకుంటున్నాడు 'he is thinking'. Literally 'he is thinking that he should go'. This is the ordinary Telugu way to say 'wants to' for an action — there is no single verb for 'want' with a verbal complement.
The first-person form of వెళ్లాలనుకుంటున్నాడు: వెళ్ళాలి + అని + అనుకుంటున్నాను 'I am thinking'. Only the final verb changes for person — the rest of the chain stays fixed.

gloss: where to go (in an embedded question)
explain: వెళ్ళాలి 'must go' with the ending -ఓ, which marks an embedded or indirect question. ఎక్కడికి వెళ్ళాలో తెలియదు is 'doesn't know where to go' — the -ఓ is what lets a question sit inside a larger sentence.

సెలవు 'leave, holiday' with the dative -కు, marking purpose — going *for* a vacation.
సెలవు 'leave, holiday' with the oblique plural -ల, here before గురించి 'about': సెలవుల గురించి, 'about the holidays'.

The borrowed 'school' with the vowel Telugu adds to consonant-final loanwords. Both స్కూల్ and స్కూలు occur; the fuller form appears before case endings.
స్కూలు 'school' with the dative -కు marking destination. Telugu adds a vowel to the borrowed స్కూల్ before the ending, giving స్కూలు-, which is a regular adaptation of consonant-final loanwords.
స్కూల్ 'school' with the locative -లో 'in, at'. -లో is the general 'inside/at' ending and attaches to borrowed and native nouns alike.
"స్నానం చేయు" = to bathe
స్నేహం 'friendship' with the adverbial -గా. Telugu often builds a manner adverb from an abstract noun this way where English would reach for an adjective like 'friendly'.
స్నేహితుడు 'friend (male)' with the plural -లు. Used for a mixed or unspecified group; the feminine singular is స్నేహితురాలు.
The English word borrowed directly. Telugu has వ్యాపకం, but that reads literary; హాబీ is what is actually said in conversation.
in "హై స్కూల్"
The English compound borrowed whole.
హైస్కూల్ with the locative -లో.

The English word borrowed whole and written in Telugu script. Everyday spoken Telugu takes many school and office terms this way. It behaves as an ordinary noun and accepts case endings: హోంవర్క్‌లో 'in the homework'.
The borrowed హోంవర్క్ with the locative -లో.
